section_title: Who are the two sisters, and why does Samaria fall?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, there were two women, daughters of the same mother, 3 and they played in Egypt, prostituting themselves from their youth. Their breasts were fondled there, and their virgin bosoms caressed. 4 The older was named Oholah, and her sister was named Oholibah. They became Mine and gave birth to sons and daughters. As for their identities, Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem.

5 Oholah prostituted herself while she was still Mine. She lusted after her lovers, the Assyrians—warriors 6 clothed in blue, governors and commanders, all desirable young men, horsemen mounted on steeds. 7 She offered sexual favors to all the elite of Assyria. She defiled herself with all the idols of those for whom she lusted. 8 She did not give up the prostitution she began in Egypt, when men slept with her in her youth, caressed her virgin bosom, and poured out their lust upon her.

9 Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, the Assyrians for whom she lusted. 10 They exposed her nakedness, seized her sons and daughters, and put her to the sword. Thus she became a byword among women, and they executed judgment against her.

context_lines: The Lord tells a story about two sisters, then identifies them: Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem. The cities stand for the two kingdoms. Their shared beginnings in Egypt lead into a picture of unfaithfulness to the God to whom they belong.

Oholah is drawn to Assyria’s impressive soldiers and rulers. Verse 7 explains what the sexual picture means: she defiles herself with their idols. The attraction to foreign power carries a betrayal of the Lord.

The power she desired becomes the power that destroys her. The Lord delivers her to the Assyrians, who take her children and put her to the sword. The reversal prepares the warning to Jerusalem: Samaria’s fate is something her sister has already seen.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/23.htm) and [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/23.htm) read the sisters as the northern and southern kingdoms, and the unfaithfulness as idolatry expressed through their dealings with other nations. The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/ezekiel/23) likewise identify the cities and their worship. The story concerns these communities’ relationship with God.

Henry and Wesley also connect the sisters’ names with their sanctuaries: Samaria’s own place of worship and the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem. [Cambridge](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezekiel/23.htm) is less certain that the names establish that contrast. The identities supplied in verse 4 are clear even where the full significance of the names is debated.
